items.title: Finding the Area of a Circle Given Its Radius

sections.normalized_html: Circle [MATH: R] has a radius of [MATH: 10] centimeters [MATH: (\mathrm{cm}).] Circle [MATH: S] has an area of [MATH: 36\pi\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}.] What is the total area, in [MATH: \mathrm{cm}^{2},] of circles [MATH: R] and [MATH: S?]
sections.readable_text: Circle [MATH: R] has a radius of [MATH: 10] centimeters [MATH: (\mathrm{cm}).] Circle [MATH: S] has an area of [MATH: 36\pi\,\mathrm{cm}^{2}.] What is the total area, in [MATH: \mathrm{cm}^{2},] of circles [MATH: R] and [MATH: S?]

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: \mathcal{A}_R] and [MATH: \mathcal{A}_S] represent the areas of circles [MATH: R] and [MATH: S,] respectively. We are given

  • Circle [MATH: R] has a radius of [MATH: 10\,\mathrm{cm}.]

  • Circle [MATH: S] has an area of [MATH: 36\pi\,\mathrm{cm}^2.]

First, we calculate the area of circle [MATH: R] using the formula for the area of a circle: [MATH: \mathcal{A} = \pi r^2]

Substituting [MATH: r = 10] into the formula, we get [MATH: A_{R}|= π ⋅ 10^{2}; = π ⋅ 100; = 100π.]

Now, we add the two areas to find the total: [MATH: A_{total}|= A_{R} + A_{S}; = 100π + 36π; = 136π]

Therefore, the total area of the two circles is [MATH: 136\pi\,\mathrm{cm}^2.]

items.title: Finding the Diameter of a Circle Given Its Circumference

sections.normalized_html: A circle has a circumference of [MATH: 72\pi] centimeters. What is the diameter, in centimeters, of the circle?
sections.readable_text: A circle has a circumference of [MATH: 72\pi] centimeters. What is the diameter, in centimeters, of the circle?

sections.normalized_html:
To find the diameter of a circle, we use the formula for circumference in terms of diameter: [MATH: C = \pi d]

We are told the circumference is [MATH: 72\pi,] so we substitute and solve for [MATH: d{:}] [MATH: 72π|= πd; d|= (72π)/(π); d|= 72]

Therefore, the diameter of the circle is [MATH: 72] centimeters.

items.title: Finding the Side Length of a Square That Has the Same Area as a Circle of Given Radius

sections.normalized_html: What is the length of one side of a square that has the same area as a circle with radius [MATH: 13] feet?
sections.readable_text: What is the length of one side of a square that has the same area as a circle with radius [MATH: 13] feet?

sections.normalized_html:
Since the radius of the circle is [MATH: 13] feet, using the formula for the area of a circle with radius [MATH: r,] we get [MATH: A_{circle}|= πr^{2}; = π ⋅ 13^{2}; = 169π.]

Now suppose a square has side length [MATH: s.] The formula for the area of a square is [MATH: \mathcal{A}_{\text{square}} = s^2.]

Since the square has the same area as the circle, we can set the two areas equal and solve for [MATH: s{:}] [MATH: A_{square}|= A_{circle}; s^{2}|= 169π; s|= sqrt(169π); = 13sqrt(π)]

Therefore, the side length of the square must be [MATH: 13\sqrt{\pi}] feet.
